subject: physics
title: Telescopes
key_idea: A telescope collects light from distant objects and makes them look bigger and brighter. A refractor uses lenses and a reflector uses mirrors. A larger diameter collects more radiation and resolves finer detail.

blocks.text: An astronomical refracting telescope uses two converging lenses. The objective collects light from a distant object. The eyepiece magnifies the image the objective forms.

items.meaning: The wide, long focal length lens that forms a real image of the distant object.
The short focal length lens that acts as a magnifying glass on that image.
The lenses are set so the final image is at infinity, which is comfortable to view.

items.text: Rays from a point on a distant object are parallel when they reach the objective.
The objective brings them to a focus in its focal plane, forming a real image.
The eyepiece is placed so its focal point is at the same place as the objective's focal point.
The eyepiece makes the rays parallel again, so the final image is at infinity.

items: The two lenses are a distance fₒ + fₑ apart.
The final image is inverted, but this does not matter for stars.
Rays leave at a larger angle to the axis than they arrived, so the image looks bigger.

blocks.text: Angular magnification compares the angle the image makes at the eye with the angle the object makes at the unaided eye.

blocks.label: Angular magnification
blocks.formula: M = angle subtended by image at eye ÷ angle subtended by object at unaided eye

blocks.label: Angular magnification in normal adjustment
where: fₒ = focal length of the objective lens (m)
fₑ = focal length of the eyepiece lens (m)

diagram.alt: A practice calculation of the angular magnification of a telescope from the two focal lengths.
diagram.question: A telescope in normal adjustment has an objective of focal length {fo} cm and an eyepiece of focal length {fe} cm. Calculate the angular magnification.

items: In normal adjustment the lenses share a focal point and the final image is at infinity.
M = fₒ ÷ fₑ, so a long objective and a short eyepiece magnify most.
Lens separation in normal adjustment is fₒ + fₑ.

blocks.text: A reflecting telescope uses a mirror instead of an objective lens. The Cassegrain arrangement folds the light path so the telescope is short.

items.text: Parallel rays hit a large parabolic concave primary mirror and are reflected towards its focus.
A small convex secondary mirror, in front of the focus, reflects the rays back towards the primary.
The rays go through a small hole in the centre of the primary mirror.
They form a real image just behind the hole, which the eyepiece magnifies.

items.meaning: Rays from the edge of a spherical lens or mirror focus at a different point from central rays, so the image is blurred.
A lens bends different colours by different amounts, so each colour focuses at a different point and the image has coloured fringes.

rows: Chromatic aberration
None, because a mirror reflects all colours the same way
Present, because a lens refracts colours differently
Spherical aberration
Removed by a parabolic mirror
Present, and hard to remove
Size
Can be very large, supported across its whole back
Large lenses sag, as they can be held only at the edge
Making it
One surface to shape and polish
Two surfaces, and the glass must be flawless all through
Light loss
Little, as light does not pass through glass
Some light is absorbed in the glass

items: A Cassegrain telescope has a parabolic concave primary and a convex secondary mirror.
Reflectors have no chromatic aberration, and a parabolic mirror removes spherical aberration.
Mirrors can be made far larger than lenses, so reflectors collect more light.

sections.heading: Radio, infrared, ultraviolet and X-ray telescopes

blocks.text: Objects give out radiation across the whole electromagnetic spectrum. Each part needs its own kind of telescope.

items: A large parabolic dish reflects radio waves to a receiver at its focus.
The dish can be a metal mesh, as the wavelength is much larger than the holes.
It is steerable, so it can track a source across the sky.
Radio waves pass through cloud and are not blocked by daylight, so it works day and night.
The signals are very weak, so a radio dish must be very large.
The atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet and X-rays, so these telescopes must be in orbit.
Infrared is absorbed by water vapour, so these telescopes are on high mountains or in space.
Infrared detectors are cooled, so the telescope's own heat does not swamp the signal.

A huge metal dish with a receiver at its focus

items: A radio dish is a parabolic reflector with a receiver at its focus.
Radio waves have long wavelengths, so a radio dish has poorer resolving power than an optical telescope of the same size.
Ultraviolet and X-ray telescopes must be above the atmosphere.

blocks.text: A larger objective or dish does two jobs. It collects more radiation and it resolves finer detail.

items.meaning: How much radiation a telescope gathers. It is proportional to the area of the aperture, so to D².
The ability to show two close sources as separate. It improves as the minimum angular resolution falls.

blocks.label: Rayleigh criterion
where: D = diameter of the telescope aperture (m)

items: Two sources can only be seen as separate if the angle between them is at least θ.
Angles here are in radians (rad). One radian is about 57°.
A larger D makes θ smaller, so finer detail is resolved.
A longer wavelength makes θ larger, which is why radio telescopes resolve poorly.
Collecting power ∝ D², so doubling the diameter collects four times the radiation and shows fainter objects.

blocks.text: The eye and the CCD as detectors

rows: Quantum efficiency
Low: only a small percentage of photons are detected
High: most photons, up to about 90%, free an electron
Resolution
Limited by the spacing of the receptor cells
Very fine, set by the tiny pixels
Convenience
Needs time to adapt to the dark and cannot store an image
Electronic output, so images are stored, added together and processed, even from far away

items: θ ≈ λ ÷ D: a larger diameter or shorter wavelength resolves finer detail.
Collecting power is proportional to D².
A CCD has higher quantum efficiency and is far more convenient than the eye.

checks.q: A telescope in normal adjustment has an objective of focal length 120 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm. Calculate its angular magnification and the distance between the lenses.
checks.a: M = fₒ ÷ fₑ = 120 ÷ 4.0 = 30. The lenses are fₒ + fₑ = 124 cm apart.

checks.q: Give two advantages of a reflecting telescope over a refracting telescope of the same aperture.
checks.a: A mirror has no chromatic aberration, as all colours reflect in the same way. A parabolic mirror removes spherical aberration. A mirror can be supported across its back, so it can be made larger without sagging. Only one surface needs to be made accurately. Any two.

checks.q: A radio telescope has a dish of diameter 64 m and detects radio waves of wavelength 0.21 m. Calculate its minimum angular resolution, and explain why it is poorer than that of an optical telescope of the same diameter.
checks.a: θ ≈ λ ÷ D = 0.21 ÷ 64 = 3.3 × 10⁻³ rad. The wavelength of radio waves is far longer than that of light, and θ is proportional to λ, so a radio telescope of the same diameter has a much larger minimum angular resolution.
